For full credit you need a comparative data quote. Pick one LVPD value, read off both rates, and state them together with both units $\text{kPa}$ and $\text{mmol m}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Check The Starting Point And Overall Trend**
Both curves start at the origin. That makes sense because LVPD is the difference in water vapour pressure between inside the leaf air spaces and outside air. If LVPD is zero there is no diffusion gradient, so no net diffusion of water vapour out, so transpiration rate is zero.

Compare Steepness And Height**
As LVPD increases, the gradient for diffusion gets steeper, so both rates increase up to $2.5 \text{ kPa}$. The solid line for H. annuus is always above the dashed line for N. oleander and rises more steeply. That fits the stem information: H. annuus is not adapted to hot dry conditions so it loses water freely, while N. oleander restricts loss.

Describe The End Of The Curves And Add Data**
Look at $2.5$ to $3.0 \text{ kPa}$. H. annuus levels off at about $10.0 \text{ mmol m}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}$. N. oleander levels off then falls slightly from about $5.1$ to $4.9 \text{ mmol m}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}$, possibly due to stomatal closure. Always quote comparatively with numbers and both units to secure the data mark.

Final answer: At $0 \text{ kPa}$ LVPD transpiration rate is $0 \text{ mmol m}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}$ for both. Both increase to $2.5 \text{ kPa}$. H. annuus has higher rate at all LVPDs and steeper rise; e.g. at $1.5 \text{ kPa}$ LVPD, H. annuus $\approx 7.2 \text{ mmol m}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}$ vs N. oleander $\approx 3.5 \text{ mmol m}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}$. Between 2.5 to $3.0 \text{ kPa}$, H. annuus plateaus at $10.0 \text{ mmol m}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}$ while N. oleander decreases slightly.

walkthrough:
Spot The Sunken Stomata In Fig. 5.3**
The lower surface is not flat. There are deep pits or crypts with stomata inside, and no stomata on the upper surface. Being underneath avoids direct sunlight and heating, but the key is the pit shape.

Explain Why Pits Conserve Water**
Water vapour diffusing out of stomata collects in the pit to form a humid pocket of still air. That lowers the difference in water vapour pressure between inside the leaf and the air just outside the stoma. A smaller gradient means slower diffusion, and wind cannot easily sweep the humid air away.

Spot Hairs And Thick Covering In Fig. 5.4**
Region N shows long hairs or trichomes growing into the pit, and the epidermal cells have very thick outer walls with a thick waxy cuticle shown as a dark layer. N. oleander also has multiple layers of thick-walled cells under the upper epidermis.

Explain Hairs And Cuticle**
Hairs trap still, humid air around the stomata, further reducing air movement and maintaining a low diffusion gradient. The thick waxy cuticle is impermeable to water, so it greatly increases diffusion distance and reduces cuticular transpiration through the epidermis.

Final answer: Fig. 5.3: stomata only on lower surface in pits / crypts / depressions. Traps humid air / still air, reduces water vapour diffusion gradient, reduces transpiration. Fig. 5.4: epidermal hairs / trichomes lining pit and thick (waxy) cuticle on thick-walled epidermis. Hairs trap water vapour / reduce air movement, cuticle is waterproof, both reduce diffusion of water vapour / cuticular transpiration.
